newsitem.title: GERMANY: German farmers opt to wait out pending flood.
newsitem.headline: German farmers opt to wait out pending flood.

text.p: As aid workers and soldiers battled day and night to prop up the dikes along the Oder River on Germany's eastern border, dozens of local farmers were ignoring evacuation calls on Monday.

With just a 70-km (40-mile) wall of dikes built 250 years ago by Frederick the Great separating the Oder river from low-lying fields of sunflowers and grains in the Oderbruch basin, any breach would spell disaster for local farmers.

Brandenburg state officials have already evacuated around 5,000 people from the region and have said that another 9,000 were "sitting on their suitcases", waiting to hear the sirens telling them that their evacuation is underway.

But farmers, many who lived through World War Two and the hardships of communist rule, are sitting tight, trying to haul in what crops can be harvested and not to let media hype or government bureaucrats make them nervous.
"We have 500 head of cattle and we haven't moved a single one out," said Joachim Schoenefeld, director of the agriculture group Agrargesellschaft Kientz mbH.

Under communism, Schoenefeld's farm was a collective with 70 workers, 540 cattle and over 6,000 pigs. Now it is a limited liability company with 12 employees, no pigs and high debts from investing in new machines.
"We haven't evacuated because of the costs of losing livestock," he said, adding that none of the local farmers had evacuated livestock or planned not to leave until the last possible minute.
A Brandenburg state official said 80 percent of cattle and dairy cows and 90 percent of pigs had been evacuated.

Frank Ehling, administrator of the Barnim-Oderbruch district of 17 villages, said unemployment in the region was over 20 percent and that a flood would hit local farmers hard, because they had to take out loans to modernise their farms.
"They have no reserve," he said. "If they lose this year's harvest they will all go broke."
Out in the fields of neighbouring farms shiny new harvesters were busily gathering grain.
Almost defiantly, fields of golden sunflowers spreading out as far as the eye can see waved gently in the low-lying basin below the menacing river that has been rising steadily.

German soldiers in their largest peace-time operation worked around the clock filling sandbags, after nearly two weeks of flooding had soaked the foundations of the dikes, rendering them soft and porous.
Further south there have been three breaks in the dike so far, flooding some 5,000 hectares (12,355 acres) of farmland in Wiesenau and Ziltendorf, south of Frankfurt an der Oder.
But if the dike bursts in the Oderbruch region, 80,000 hectares of farmland and 24 villages would be submerged in the basin that is some 50 km (30 Miles) long and 17 km (11 Miles) wide.
Heinz-Dieter Nieschke, head of the Brandenburg state farmer's association, said local residents had tough nerves because they have lived next to the river for years.
"If the dike breaks it will be a catastrophe. We all know that," he said. "But it doesn't mean that we won't be able to plant winter grains in the fall. We have to wait and see."
The German government has contacted the European Union, hoping to gain approval for a quick emergency aid programme for local farmers.
"We want to tell farmers clearly that they will receive unbureaucratic assistance," said German Farm Minister Jochen Borchert during a whistle-stop tour of local farms.
